title: Software testing
summary: The practice of checking that code behaves as specified through repeatable automated checks written at the cheapest level that can catch the defect.

misconceptions.text: High line coverage means the code is correct.

explain: states what a test asserts and what it cannot assert
names at least three test levels and says what each one isolates
explains why a suite is a design constraint and not only a safety net
apply: writes a failing test before the fix and shows it turn green
chooses the cheapest level that can catch the defect
keeps each test independent of execution order and shared state
discriminate: separates a unit test from an integration test by what it isolates
separates coverage from correctness with one concrete example
separates a flaky test from a genuinely failing test by the evidence

title: JSON Schema
summary: A declarative vocabulary for constraining the shape of JSON documents so an invalid payload is rejected before it reaches application code.

misconceptions.text: If the property types match, the payload is valid.

explain: distinguishes type, required and additionalProperties by what each one rejects
names one invariant a schema cannot express, such as a cross field rule
describes what a validator returns on failure and how a caller uses it
apply: writes a schema that rejects a named bad payload and accepts the good one
sets additionalProperties to false where the interface is closed
uses enum or const instead of a free string where the value set is fixed
discriminate: separates schema validation from business rule validation
separates a schema that constrains from one that only documents
separates a parse failure from a validation failure

title: Tool calling
summary: The mechanism by which a model requests a named function with structured arguments and then has to interpret the structured result it gets back.

misconceptions.text: The model runs the tool itself, so the application cannot refuse the call.

explain: describes the round trip from tool declaration to arguments to result
states that the application, not the model, decides whether to execute
explains what happens when arguments do not match the declared schema
apply: declares a tool with a schema the model can fill without extra prose
handles a malformed or missing argument without throwing to the caller
returns a result the model can act on, with a status field and no free text blob
discriminate: separates the call protocol from the design of the tool interface
separates a tool result from a model assertion about the world
separates a refused call from a failed call in the trace

title: Unit testing
summary: Isolated checks of one function or module with its collaborators replaced, fast enough to run on every save.

explain: states what is replaced at the unit boundary and why
explains why a unit test must not depend on network or clock
says what a unit test proves about the whole system, which is little
apply: replaces one collaborator with a double and asserts on the observable result
names the test after the behaviour rather than after the function
covers the boundary case that motivated the code, not only the happy path
discriminate: separates a unit test from a task level agent eval by what fails when it fails
separates a stub from a mock by what each one asserts
separates a slow unit test from an integration test that is mislabelled

title: Agent loop
summary: The cycle of observe, decide, act and record that turns a single model call into a process able to make progress across many steps.

misconceptions.text: An agent loop is a retry loop around one prompt.

explain: names the four phases and what carries information between them
states what makes the loop terminate, including the failure exits
explains why the record phase is what makes the next decision better
apply: writes a loop with an explicit step budget and a stop condition
passes the tool result back as evidence rather than as a new instruction
records each step so the run can be read afterwards
discriminate: separates the loop from the state it reads and writes
separates a planning step from an acting step in a trace
separates a loop that makes progress from one that repeats itself

title: Tool interface design
summary: Choosing the name, schema, description and return shape of a tool so a model can call it correctly without reading the implementation.

misconceptions.text: Adding more tools always makes the agent more capable.

explain: explains why the description is part of the interface and not documentation
states why a closed schema reduces the number of invalid calls
describes how the return shape changes what the model does next
apply: rewrites an ambiguous tool name and description into an unambiguous pair
collapses two overlapping tools into one with an explicit mode argument
returns a structured error the model can recover from instead of a thrown exception
discriminate: separates interface design from the transport that carries the call
separates a missing capability from a badly described one
separates a tool the model misuses from a tool the model should not have

title: Acceptance criteria
summary: Concrete checkable statements of what a finished task must satisfy, written before the work starts.

explain: states why a criterion must be checkable by someone who did not do the work
explains what a criterion excludes as well as what it requires
says who writes them and at what point in the task
apply: turns a vague request into three criteria with an observable verdict each
writes one criterion that would fail a plausible wrong solution
keeps implementation choices out of the criteria
discriminate: separates an acceptance criterion from a rubric line used for scoring
separates a criterion from a preference stated as a requirement
separates done from good enough for this task

title: Context design
summary: Deciding what information enters the model window at each step, in what order, and what is deliberately left out.

misconceptions.text: More context always improves the agent.

explain: explains how irrelevant context changes the model's ranking of next actions
names the cost of context in tokens, latency and attention dilution
states one rule for what to drop when the window is full
apply: cuts a bloated prompt and shows the task still passes its checks
orders the context so the task statement is not buried by evidence
marks which blocks are untrusted data rather than instructions
discriminate: separates context design from long term memory design
separates retrieval quality from placement in the window
separates a prompt that lacks information from one that has too much

title: Feedback loops
summary: Structures that return the result of an action to the agent so the next decision is corrected by evidence instead of by guessing.

misconceptions.text: Showing the agent its own output counts as a feedback loop.

explain: names the signal, the channel and the decision the signal changes
explains why a loop with no verdict in it is not a feedback loop
states what makes a loop converge rather than oscillate
apply: adds a check whose verdict reaches the agent before its next action
shortens a loop so the correction happens in the same run
shows one run where the loop changed the agent's second attempt
discriminate: separates feedback from feedforward by when the information arrives
separates a verdict returned to the agent from a log written for a human
separates recovery from feedback by what each one restores

title: Feedforward
summary: Information given to the agent before it acts, such as the target, the constraints and the shape of a good answer, so fewer corrections are needed later.

misconceptions.text: Feedforward is just writing a longer prompt.

explain: states that feedforward arrives before the action and feedback after it
names three things worth stating in advance, such as the target and the format
explains why a worked example is feedforward and a score is not
apply: rewrites a task brief so the success condition is stated before the first action
supplies the answer shape and one counterexample up front
shows the attempt count dropping after the brief is improved
discriminate: separates feedforward from feedback by the moment it is delivered
separates a constraint given in advance from a correction given afterwards
separates acceptance criteria from the feedforward that carries them

title: State management
summary: Keeping the facts a run depends on in an explicit store that survives a step boundary, a retry or a restart.

misconceptions.text: The conversation transcript is a good enough place to keep state.

explain: names what belongs in explicit state rather than in the transcript
explains what a step boundary is and what must survive it
states how state is reconciled after a partial failure
apply: moves a fact out of the transcript into a keyed store and reads it back
makes one step idempotent so a retry does not duplicate its effect
writes state before the side effect, not after it
discriminate: separates run state from long lived memory
separates state the agent may write from state only the system may write
separates a lost fact from a fact the agent chose to ignore

title: Threat modeling
summary: Enumerating who can influence a system, what they want and which trust boundaries their input crosses, before choosing any mitigation.

misconceptions.text: Threat modeling is running through a checklist of known vulnerabilities.

explain: names actor, asset, trust boundary and abuse case as separate things
explains why the model comes before the mitigation list
states how a threat model is invalidated by a design change
apply: draws the trust boundaries of an agent that reads the web and writes to a repository
lists three abuse cases with the actor and the asset named in each
ranks them by impact and by how cheap the mitigation is
discriminate: separates a threat from a vulnerability and from a mitigation
separates the attack surface from the threat model that reasons about it
separates an untrusted input from an input that is merely unvalidated

title: Deterministic verification
summary: Checking a result with code that returns the same verdict every time, so the check itself never has to be trusted twice.

misconceptions.text: A model judge is a fine substitute for a deterministic check.

explain: states what makes a check deterministic, including the absence of a model in it
explains why a deterministic verdict can gate an action and a scored one cannot
names one property that cannot be checked deterministically
apply: replaces a judged criterion with an executable check that returns pass or fail
pins the inputs so the same run gives the same verdict twice
keeps the check independent of the code path that produced the result
discriminate: separates a deterministic check from a rubric score
separates a check that is flaky from one that is genuinely failing
separates verification of the output from verification of the process

title: Regression testing
summary: Re-running a pinned set of cases after every change so a fix that breaks earlier behaviour is caught at the moment it is introduced.

explain: explains why a case is added to the suite when a bug is found, not before
states what pinning means and why the expected values are stored
says how the suite is kept fast enough to actually run
apply: adds the failing case to the suite before fixing the defect
pins the expected output and shows the diff on a regression
quarantines a flaky case instead of deleting the signal
discriminate: separates a regression from a new requirement
separates a pinned expectation from a golden file nobody reviews
separates a regression suite from an eval set

title: Human in the loop
summary: Placing an explicit human decision point in an automated flow at the steps where a wrong action is expensive or irreversible.

misconceptions.text: Adding an approval prompt to every action makes the system safe.

explain: names the two properties that make a step worth interrupting, cost and reversibility
explains how approval fatigue turns a control into a rubber stamp
states what the human must see for the decision to be real
apply: picks the one step in a flow that deserves an approval and justifies the choice
shows the human the exact effect, not a summary of it
records the decision with who made it and what was shown
discriminate: separates an approval gate from a permission boundary enforced by code
separates a human decision from a human notification
separates a control that changes behaviour from one that only reassures

title: Cost and latency
summary: Treating tokens, wall clock time and tool round trips as a budget that shapes the design rather than a number to look at afterwards.

explain: names the three budgets, tokens, time and round trips, and how they trade off
explains why the step count usually dominates the per call cost
states where caching changes the shape of the budget
apply: measures one run and attributes its cost to steps rather than to the total
removes one round trip and shows the task still passes
sets a step budget that fails the run instead of spending without a bound
discriminate: separates a slow model from a chatty loop
separates cost per run from cost per successful run
separates a context problem from a latency problem

title: Rubric grading
summary: Scoring open ended work against named criteria that a second grader could apply to the same answer and reach the same verdict.

misconceptions.text: A rubric score is a measurement, so it can be compared across rubrics.

explain: states what makes a criterion independently checkable by two graders
explains why a rubric line must describe observable evidence, not quality
says how disagreement between graders is used to fix the rubric
apply: turns a vague quality into three criteria with a yes or no verdict each
grades one answer and shows which criterion each verdict came from
revises a criterion that two graders read differently
discriminate: separates a rubric score from a deterministic pass or fail
separates a criterion about evidence from one about style
separates grader disagreement from learner error

title: Agent evals
summary: Task level evaluation of an agent's end to end behaviour, as opposed to unit tests of its functions.

misconceptions.text: If the unit tests pass, the agent works.

explain: states what an eval measures that a unit test cannot, which is task completion
names the three parts of an eval case, the task, the environment and the verdict
explains why an eval needs a deterministic verdict to be comparable over time
apply: writes one eval case with a task, a fixed environment and an executable check
adds a task level check to a harness that already has passing unit tests
reports the result as a rate over cases rather than as a single run
discriminate: distinguishes deterministic function checks from task level agent evaluation
mentions end to end behaviour
gives one example where unit tests pass but the agent fails

title: Observability
summary: Emitting enough structured signal from a running agent that a question about a past run can be answered without reproducing it.

misconceptions.text: If everything is logged, the system is observable.

explain: states the question first and the signal needed to answer it second
names what must be on every step record, such as the step id and the inputs
explains why unstructured logs cannot answer a question about a rate
apply: adds a structured step record with a stable id and correlates two steps by it
emits the tool arguments and the verdict, not only the final answer
answers one concrete question from stored records without rerunning the agent
discriminate: separates emitting signal from reading a trace
separates a metric from an example
separates a missing signal from a signal nobody queried

title: Harness iteration
summary: Improving the scaffolding around the model, the tools, the briefs and the checks, instead of reaching for a bigger model when a task fails.

misconceptions.text: A failing task means the model is not good enough.

explain: names three parts of the harness that can be changed before the model is
explains why a change is kept only when the eval rate moves
states how one change at a time keeps the attribution honest
apply: diagnoses a failing run and names the harness part responsible
makes one change, reruns the eval set and reports the rate before and after
reverts a change that did not move the rate
discriminate: separates a harness defect from a model capability limit
separates iterating on the harness from iterating on the eval set
separates a real improvement from noise across a small case set

title: Attack surface
summary: The complete set of inputs, tools and side channels through which an untrusted party can influence what an agent does.

misconceptions.text: Only what the user types is untrusted input.

explain: lists the entry points of an agent, including tool results and retrieved documents
explains why every write capable tool widens the surface twice, on read and on write
states how the surface changes when a new tool is added
apply: enumerates the surface of a given agent and marks each entry trusted or untrusted
identifies the two entry points that carry the most authority
proposes one reduction that removes an entry point rather than filtering it
discriminate: separates the attack surface from a specific attack such as injection
separates an entry point from a vulnerability at that point
separates surface reduction from input filtering

title: Prompt injection
summary: An attack in which text the agent reads as data is treated as instructions, usually arriving through a tool result the agent already trusts.

misconceptions.text: Telling the model to ignore injected instructions prevents prompt injection.

explain: names the path from untrusted source to context to action
explains why the model cannot reliably tell data from instructions
states why a mitigation must sit outside the model to hold
apply: marks which entries in a given trace are untrusted and which action they reached
adds one control outside the model, such as an allowlist or a confirmation
shows the same payload failing after the control is added
discriminate: separates injection at the input from unvalidated output at the exit
separates a jailbreak of the assistant from an injection through a tool result
separates a prompt level mitigation from an enforced one

title: Permission boundaries
summary: The explicit line between what an agent may do without asking and what needs a separate authority, enforced outside the model.

misconceptions.text: A rule in the system prompt is a permission boundary.

explain: states where the boundary is enforced and by which component
explains why a boundary written in the prompt is advice, not enforcement
names what crosses the boundary, the authority rather than the request
apply: splits a tool set into a group that runs freely and a group that needs authority
enforces the split in the tool layer and shows a denied call
records the denial so it can be read afterwards
discriminate: separates a boundary from a least privilege grant inside it
separates enforcement in code from an instruction to the model
separates an approval gate for a human from a boundary between components

title: Recovery
summary: Returning a run to a known good state after a failed step, by retry, compensation or rollback, without losing what was already verified.

misconceptions.text: Retrying the failed step is a recovery strategy.

explain: names retry, compensation and rollback and when each one applies
explains why a non idempotent side effect cannot simply be retried
states what a known good state means for a given run
apply: adds a compensating action for a step that cannot be rolled back
makes a retry safe by keying the side effect on a stable id
shows a run that fails mid way and resumes without repeating verified work
discriminate: separates recovery from retrying the same call again
separates a recoverable failure from one that must stop the run
separates the failure taxonomy from the recovery it selects

title: Memory design
summary: Choosing what an agent keeps across runs, in what form, and what causes it to be written, read or forgotten.

misconceptions.text: Memory is just a larger context window.

explain: names the write trigger, the read trigger and the forget rule as separate decisions
explains why unbounded memory degrades rather than improves behaviour
states how a stale memory is detected
apply: defines what is written after a run and what is deliberately dropped
reads memory into the window only when a named trigger fires
expires or supersedes an entry rather than accumulating contradictions
discriminate: separates memory from run state that dies with the run
separates memory from retrieval over an external corpus
separates a stale memory from a wrong one

title: Retrieval augmentation
summary: Fetching relevant documents at query time and placing them in the context so an answer is grounded in a source that can be cited.

misconceptions.text: If the document is in the context, the answer is grounded in it.

explain: names the three stages, index, retrieve and place, and what fails at each
explains why recall and precision pull the chunk size in opposite directions
states how a citation is checked rather than assumed
apply: chooses a chunking rule for a given corpus and justifies it with one failure case
measures whether the retrieved passage actually contains the answer
requires a citation and rejects an answer whose citation does not support it
discriminate: separates retrieval failure from generation failure using the retrieved text
separates retrieval from memory by where the content lives
separates a grounded answer from one that merely quotes

title: Tool result provenance
summary: Tracking where each piece of content in an agent's context came from, so trusted and untrusted material can be treated differently.

explain: states why provenance has to travel with the content and not beside it
explains what changes once a block is labelled untrusted
names one decision that should read the label before acting
apply: labels each context block with its source and trust level
blocks an action whose only justification came from an untrusted block
keeps the label through a summarisation step
discriminate: separates provenance from validation of the content itself
separates a trusted source from a verified claim
separates a labelled block from a quoted one

title: Trace analysis
summary: Reading a recorded run step by step to locate the first decision that went wrong rather than the step where the error surfaced.

misconceptions.text: The step that threw the error is the step that caused the failure.

explain: explains why the first wrong decision is usually earlier than the visible error
names what to read at each step, the inputs, the choice and the verdict
states how two runs are compared to isolate the difference
apply: walks a failing trace and marks the first step whose decision was wrong
quotes the evidence in that step that should have changed the decision
names the harness change that would have prevented it
discriminate: separates reading a trace from emitting the signal that made it readable
separates the first wrong decision from the last error
separates a single trace finding from a pattern across runs

title: Failure taxonomy
summary: A named and mutually exclusive set of failure modes that makes counts comparable across runs and points at a specific fix.

explain: states why categories must be mutually exclusive to be counted
explains how a category is tied to the part of the harness that owns it
says what happens to the taxonomy when a new failure does not fit
apply: labels twenty failed runs with a taxonomy of at most six categories
reports the counts and names the category worth fixing first
splits a category that turned out to hide two different causes
discriminate: separates a failure mode from a single failing trace
separates a symptom category from a cause category
separates a rare category from a badly defined one

title: Sandboxing
summary: Running agent actions inside an environment whose reachable resources are limited by the runtime, not by the agent's intentions.

misconceptions.text: Running the code in a container makes it sandboxed.

explain: names what a sandbox limits, the filesystem, the network and the process table
explains why the limit must be enforced by the runtime and not requested by the code
states what escapes a sandbox, such as a shared credential or a mounted path
apply: chooses the resources an agent task actually needs and denies the rest by default
shows one denied operation and what the agent does after the denial
keeps the credential outside the sandbox and passes a scoped token in
discriminate: separates sandboxing, which limits reach, from least privilege, which limits grant
separates isolation from filtering
separates a sandbox from a sandbox with a shared writable mount

title: Least privilege
summary: Granting each component only the authority its current task needs, for only as long as it needs it.

misconceptions.text: Read only access cannot cause damage.

explain: states the two dimensions of a grant, the scope and the duration
explains why a read grant can still leak an asset
names how a grant is revoked when the task ends
apply: rewrites a broad token into a task scoped one and names what it can no longer do
sets an expiry that matches the task rather than the session
shows the agent completing the task under the narrower grant
discriminate: separates a narrow grant from an isolated environment
separates least privilege from asking for approval
separates a scoped credential from a filtered interface over a broad one

title: Output validation
summary: Checking what comes back from a model or a tool against a schema and a policy before any of it is allowed to affect the world.

misconceptions.text: If the output parses against the schema, it is safe to act on.

explain: separates shape validation from policy validation and says why both are needed
explains why validation belongs at the exit, before the side effect
states what the system does with an output that fails, other than retrying
apply: validates a tool argument against a closed schema and rejects an extra field
adds a policy check, such as an allowlisted destination, on top of the schema
shows an injected instruction failing at the exit even though it parsed
discriminate: separates validating what comes out from sanitising what goes in
separates a schema violation from a policy violation
separates a rejected output from a retried one

title: Red teaming
summary: Deliberately attacking your own agent with adversarial inputs to find failures that ordinary evaluation will never produce.

misconceptions.text: A red team pass at the end of the project is enough.

explain: states what a red team run produces, a reproducible attack case, not an opinion
explains why attacks are written against the surface, entry point by entry point
says how a found attack becomes a permanent regression case
apply: writes three attack cases against named entry points of a given agent
records one successful attack as a reproducible case with the expected refusal
adds the case to the suite so a regression is caught later
discriminate: separates red teaming from evaluating normal task performance
separates an attack case from a threat model entry
separates a real bypass from a refusal that only looks like one

title: Eval dataset design
summary: Assembling a set of tasks whose coverage, difficulty and answer keys make an eval score mean something over time.

misconceptions.text: A larger eval set is always a better eval set.

explain: explains why coverage of failure modes matters more than raw case count
states how a saturated set stops distinguishing two harnesses
names the risk of tuning on the same set the score is reported from
apply: selects cases so each known failure mode has at least two of them
holds out a slice and reports the rate on it separately
retires a case that every version now passes and records why
discriminate: separates the dataset from the eval harness that runs it
separates an eval set from a regression suite by what each protects
separates a hard case from a badly specified one
